contents: # Team (uhifadhi/team-module) — who this installation's people are and how they
# sign in.
# TWO KEYS, AND NEITHER OF THEM IS SECURITY. What a deployment usually wants to
# change about signing in — who may reach what, how long a session lives,
# whether there is a remember-me cookie, how hard passwords are hashed — is not
# here and cannot be: it is `config/packages/security.yaml`, which this bundle's
# recipe also wrote and which belongs to YOU. Firewalls and access_control are
# application configuration by Symfony's own design.
# What IS here is the two things the SCREEN needs and a firewall has no opinion
# about. The tree is closed, so an invented key fails loudly.
team:
# Where a visitor who asks for /login while already signed in is sent.
# A PATH, NOT A ROUTE NAME. The bundle cannot know what you call your home
# screen, and a route name it guessed wrong would be a 500 at the exact
# moment somebody finally got their password right. Where a FRESH sign-in
# lands is a different setting and lives in the firewall
# (form_login.default_target_path).
after_sign_in_path: '/'
# The sentence under the mark on the sign-in card. Say who you are here
# rather than by patching a template out of the vendor tree.
sign_in_lede: 'Analytical observatory for protected areas. Sign in to reach this installation and its modules.'
# The two addresses uhifadhi/team-module owns: /login and /logout.
# A MODULE MAY SHIP ROUTES — only the shell may not. The controller carries its
# own #[Route] attributes; this file is where your application mounts them, and
# it is yours: prefix them, restrict them, or point somewhere else entirely.
# THE ROUTE NAMES MATTER. `config/packages/security.yaml` names `team_login` and
# `team_logout` in its form_login and logout keys, so if you drop this file the
# firewall has nothing to point at and the container will say so at compile time.
team:
resource: '@UhifadhiTeamBundle/src/Controller/'
type: attribute
